0.1 We first make explicit the full physical DN map and the identity on a possibly disconnected $\Omega$. The compact smooth manifold $\overline\Omega$ has finitely many connected components $M_a=\overline\Omega_a$, $1\le a\le J$: connected coordinate neighborhoods give an open cover, and a finite subcover meets every component. Each $M_a$ has nonempty boundary; otherwise its same-dimensional inclusion in $\mathbb R^n$ would make it both open and compact, impossible for a nonempty subset of $\mathbb R^n$. Thus the connected-domain suppliers [F1] and [F2] apply on every $M_a$. Fixed finite atlases identify $H^1(\Omega)=\bigoplus_aH^1(\Omega_a)$ and $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)=\bigoplus_aH^{1/2}(\partial\Omega_a)$, with the corresponding finite sum for the boundary dual. The full physical map is $\Lambda_\gamma=\bigoplus_a\Lambda_{\gamma|_{M_a}}$: solve separately on each component, and its weak boundary pairing is the sum of the component weak pairings. This is exactly the global physical flux pairing, not an additional assumption on the conductivities or data. Equality of the global maps implies equality of the component maps by inputs and tests supported on one component. Applying [F2] on each component and summing gives the global Alessandrini identity used below. The quasimode supplier [F3], Proof 5.1, already constructs the exact solutions componentwise. Boundary normal collars and derivatives are componentwise as well. Consequently all later localization and normal-jet steps apply without a connectedness restriction. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, given, construct, algebra]

proposed_edits.source_excerpt: 1.1 Apply [F1] to choose an admissible finite code for a regular diagram of a representative of $K$, and choose a basepoint in the interior of one edge. There is such an edge because a one-component code has at least one edge, including in the crossing-free case. [A1, F1, given, choose]
proposed_edits.proposed_replacement: 1.1 Apply [F1] to choose an admissible finite code for a regular diagram of a representative of $K$, and choose a basepoint in the interior of one edge away from every crossing and geometric bend. There is such a point: a one-component code has at least one nondegenerate polygonal edge segment, including in the crossing-free case, and only finitely many crossings and bends are forbidden. Choose an interior point of such a segment outside that finite set. [A1, F1, given, choose]

proposed_edits.source_excerpt: 2.1 If $L$ is the unknot, [F2] forces both diagrams to have zero crossings. A connected crossing-free diagram is one embedded oriented circle on the projection sphere, and the two such circles are carried to one another by a sphere planar isotopy with their orientations transported. This proves the conclusion in this case. Henceforth $L$ is nontrivial and both diagrams have positive crossing count. [given, F2, F6, step 1.1, construct]
proposed_edits.proposed_replacement: 2.1 If $L$ is empty, both diagrams are empty, and the identity sphere planar isotopy proves the conclusion. Henceforth assume $L$ is nonempty. If $L$ is the unknot, [F2] forces both diagrams to have zero crossings. A connected crossing-free diagram is one embedded oriented circle on the projection sphere, and the two such circles are carried to one another by a sphere planar isotopy with their orientations transported. This proves the conclusion in this case. Henceforth $L$ is nontrivial and both diagrams have positive crossing count. [given, F2, F6, step 1.1, construct]
